meaning: Titan of warcraft; father of Nike, Kratos, Bia, and Zelos

phonemes.desc: Voiceless labial stop plus alpha with acute: the stressed syllable rises in pitch.

pronunciation.approximation: 'PAHL-lahs' — the first syllable carries the ancient Greek pitch accent.
pronunciation.note: Pállas is a short, sharp name whose acute on the first syllable gives it a commander's ring. The meaning is uncertain; ancient sources connect it with 'brandish' (πάλλω) or 'spear'.

domains.title: Titan of Warcraft
domains.subtitle: Strategy, the Spear, and the Art of Battle
domains.lead: Pállas is the Titan who embodies the craft of war itself — not mere berserk rage but the disciplined art of spear, shield, and strategy. He is the father of Nike (Victory), Kratos (Strength), Bia (Force), and Zelos (Rivalry): war produces its own children, and they never leave his household.

cards.name: The Spear
cards.desc: His signature weapon, cast in celestial bronze, the metal of the gods.

cards.name: Strategy
cards.desc: War as calculation: the arrangement of forces before the clash.

cards.name: Father of Personifications
cards.desc: Nike, Kratos, Bia, and Zelos are born from his lineage.

cards.name: Celestial Bronze
cards.desc: The divine alloy that marks the armament of gods and Titans.

symbols.name: Spear

symbols.name: Shield
symbols.meaning: Defense as part of the art of battle

symbols.name: Celestial bronze

mythology.lead: Pállas belongs to the older generation of gods, the Titans. His myth is less narrative than genealogical and thematic: he is the source from which the personifications of war's consequences descend.

myths.title: Son of Kreios and Eurybia
myths.text: Hesiod names Pállas as the son of the Titan Kreios (Crius) and the sea-power Eurybia. From this union of sky-lineage and maritime force comes a deity whose domain is the practical mastery of conflict.

myths.title: The Children of Pállas
myths.text: By the Oceanid Styx, Pállas fathers Nike (Victory), Kratos (Strength), Bia (Force), and Zelos (Rivalry). These are not companions chosen at random; they are the necessary entourage of any war. Where Pállas is, they follow.

myths.title: War in Heaven
myths.text: As a Titan, Pállas belongs to the older order overthrown by Zeus and the Olympians. His children, however, side with Zeus — a sign that the forces of warcraft can be transferred from one regime to the next.

lore.syncretism: Pállas is often conflated in the modern imagination with Pallas Athena, whose cult title 'Pallas' may originally have been separate. Some ancient sources suggest Athena slew a giant or Titan named Pallas and took his name as a trophy. The overlap has made 'Pallas' ambiguous: it can mean the Titan of warcraft, or it can be an epithet of Athena. PUNICODEX treats them as distinct entries, each with its own temple and domain.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name Pállas survives most famously in 'Pallas Athena', but the Titan himself represents the older, pre-Olympian concept of war as a craft and lineage. In modern military, strategy, and sportswear branding, his name signals disciplined force and competitive edge. As father of Nike, Kratos, Bia, and Zelos, he is the genealogical root of several personifications still active in English vocabulary.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Pállas is war as a technology. He is not the bloodlust of Árēs nor the strategic wisdom of Athēnâ; he is the craft itself — the forging of weapons, the drilling of formations, the transmission of technique from one generation of fighters to the next. His children are not emotions but outcomes: victory, strength, force, rivalry.

To think about Pállas is to ask whether war can ever be pure craft, divorced from the reasons for which it is fought. The Greeks suspected not; even a craftsman of battle must eventually choose a side. His children followed Zeus, and so, in the end, did the craft.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Greek as Πάλλας. The acute accent falls on the first alpha. PUNICODEX restores this as Pállas; the ASCII form 'pallas' flattens the pitch accent that ancient Greek speakers would have heard.
